newsitem.title: USA: EPA says will issue mercury study this year.
newsitem.headline: EPA says will issue mercury study this year.

text.p: The Environmental Protection Agency plans to release a long-awaited study on risks and sources of mercury pollution by the end of the year, an EPA official said Thursday.
A group of senators in a resolution earlier Thursday called on the agency to immediately release the 1,700-page report that originally was due in November 1994.
But EPA Assistant Administrator Mary Nichols said parts of the report were not yet finished. "We expect it will be done before the end of the year," she said.
The study, which in a 1995 draft drew fire from electric utilities and the fishing industry, has had "substantial changes" as it was reviewed by the agency's Science Advisory Board, Nichols said.
She said the report was sent to the board to incorporate information from new government-funded studies.

But critics including the Sierra Club Legal Defence Fund, which sued the agency to release the report, said it was completed in late 1995, then withheld because of pressure from electric utilities that were tagged as significant mercury polluters.

Sen. Patrick Leahy, a Vermont Democrat who sponsored the resolution, complained that the EPA withheld timely information that was vital to state and federal regulators in revising health standards, air pollution controls and plans to increase competition among electric utilities.

He and six other senators pushed a resolution calling for the report's immediate release, for the EPA to begin landfill testing in selected sites across the country, and for the agency to include mercury lamps in hazardous waste rules.
Last fall, 22 senators and 25 representatives signed letters to EPA Administrator Carol Browner urging her to release the 1,700-page report.
Sources of mercury pollution include power plants, waste incinerators, improper disposal of mercury-containing lamps and batteries, and natural sources.

Thirty-seven states have issued advisories on consuming mercury-tainted freshwater fish, and the EPA estimate that some 80,000 pregnant women each year are exposed to mercury levels that pose risks to their children.

The Edison Electric Institute, which represents investor-owned utilities, complained that the first draft of the report focused on an acute poisoning event in Iraq, and put an unfair share of the blame for mercury emissions on utilities, institute spokeswoman Linda Schoumacher said.
She said she understood some of the utility industry's concerns on models the study used to discern pollution sources had been alleviated in the current draft.
